title: Near-optimal quantum metrology with few-qubit measurements
authors: Liang Mao, Senrui Chen, Hsin-Yuan Huang, John Preskill, Sisi Zhou
abstract: Quantum metrology, which addresses parameter estimation in quantum systems, has broad applications across science and technology. Conventional metrology protocols for multi-qubit states in the multi-parameter regime typically require highly complex quantum measurements, leading to substantial quantum-resource costs. In this work, we introduce a family of metrology protocols that use only few-qubit measurements, thereby significantly reducing the required resources. For arbitrary pure states, one of our protocols approaches the quantum Cramér-Rao bound up to an overhead in sample complexity that scales linearly with the number of qubits, irrespective of the number of parameters to be estimated. For typical Haar-random states, this overhead can be reduced to a constant. Our results build on recent advances in quantum state certification protocols with few-qubit measurements: we establish a universal connection between certification and metrology in which the precision of the certification protocol determines the metrological overhead. We also illustrate our approach through an example of Hamiltonian estimation from ground states.
summary: This paper introduces new quantum metrology protocols designed to estimate parameters in multi-qubit systems while drastically reducing the complexity of required quantum measurements. By establishing a link between state certification and parameter estimation, they show that few-qubit measurements can achieve near-optimal precision relative to the ultimate QFI bound. This is highly relevant for building practical, resource-efficient quantum sensors.
main_problem: To develop quantum metrology protocols that estimate unknown parameters encoded in a quantum state using only physically feasible few-qubit measurements.
main_result: The authors establish a universal connection between quantum state certification and metrology, achieving near-optimal precision approaching the Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound with measurement overhead scaling favorably (constant for Haar random states).
method: They transform protocols based on Conditional Fidelity Estimation (CFE) from state certification into metrological estimation frameworks using specific POVMs derived from few-qubit measurements.
model_or_system: The study analyzes parameter estimation for parameterized pure quantum states $|\psi(	heta)angle$ in a multi-qubit Hilbert space, exemplified by Hamiltonian estimation problems.
key_observables: Mean Squared Error Matrix (MSEM), Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), and the Certification Gap ($\Delta$).
important_parameters: Number of qubits ($n$), number of parameters ($m$), and measurement overhead scaling factors ($\mathcal{O}(n)$ or constant).
main_assumptions: The protocols rely on establishing bounds derived from state certification techniques, particularly for Haar-random states.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the comparison between general quantum metrology POVMs and the proposed few-qubit measurement protocols; other figures show scaling of MSE vs. measurement number or CFI/QFI traces vs. system size $n$.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first defining the problem using QCRB, then introducing CFE as a link to metrology (Lemma 1), and finally deriving specific bounds for non-adaptive (Markov chain mixing time) and adaptive (Decision Tree) measurements, culminating in results for Haar random states.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, resource-efficient measurement strategies that bridge the gap between theoretical quantum limits (QFI) and practical experimental feasibility using limited local measurements, which is crucial for designing real quantum sensors.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of quantum metrology and our measurement protocol. (a) In quantum metrology, a POVM {Mx}x is performed on the state |ψ(θ)⟩. Upon the outcome x, classical computer builds an estimator ˆθ. In quantum metrol- ogy, one typically has access to a prior estimate θ0 that is close to the true value θ. (b) In our protocol, the POVM acts locally on n−r qubits and as a random Clifford measurement on r qubits. Throughout the protocols introduced this work, r is at most O(log n). In most cases, r = 1 is sufficient.
